PAPER: QUESTIONNAIRES APPLICATION Published Online: November 10, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multirev.2026276 The impact of innovation capabilities on SME performance in emerging markets: Evidence from Indonesia Yuni Setyawatia | Armanu Armanub | Mugiono Mugionob | Kusuma Ratnawatib aManagement Department, Faculty of Economics, Tribhuwana Tunggadewi University, Malang, Indonesia. bDoctoral Program in Management, Faculty of Economics and Business, Brawijaya University, Malang, Indonesia. Abstract Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are key drivers of economic growth in emerging markets; however, their performance is often constrained by limited resources, technology gaps, and low innovation capabilities. While innovation capability is widely recognized as a determinant of business success, its influence on SME performance in emerging economies remains underexplored. This study examines the effect of three dimensions of innovation capability—product innovation capability, process innovation capability, and market innovation capability—on the performance of SMEs in the manufacturing subsectors of East Java, Indonesia. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from 160 SMEs using purposive sampling. Structured questionnaires were used to obtain responses, and the data were analysed using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) approach. The findings reveal that process innovation capability (β = 0.290, p < 0.05) and market innovation capability (β = 0.414, p < 0.05) have a significant positive impact on SME performance, highlighting the importance of internal process efficiency and responsiveness to market demands. In contrast, product innovation capability shows no significant effect (β = 0.049, p > 0.05), suggesting that new product development is not yet a primary driver of performance in this context. Theoretically, this study extends the dynamic capabilities framework within the context of emerging-market SMEs. Practically, it highlights the importance of strategic alignment between operational processes and market orientation to strengthen competitiveness, sustain profitability, and achieve long-term business resilience. These findings offer valuable implications for SME owners, policymakers, and support institutions aiming to foster innovation-driven growth within developing economies. Keywords: dynamic approach, product development, process efficiency, market adaptability, firm competitiveness 1. Introduction SMEs are widely recognized as engines of economic growth and pillars of development in nearly all economies. In developing countries, economic performance largely depends on the contributions of SMEs (Fu et al., 2021). SMEs are often regarded as drivers of growth because of their role in supporting entrepreneurial activities and fostering innovation, which in turn enhances competition and productivity. The relatively high flexibility and adaptability of SMEs to market changes enables them to be more creative and responsive than larger firms are (Prima Lita et al., 2020). In today’s business environment, traditional business models are no longer sustainable in the long term and must be continuously innovated. Firms that manage to survive in the marketplace are those that consistently deliver value to consumers through the development of innovative business models (Fu et al., 2021). For SMEs, innovation is a crucial strategy for improving performance and remaining competitive. It plays a central role in product development, contributes to business growth, and creates opportunities for greater profitability and competitiveness. However, innovation often provides only temporary advantages, as successful ideas are likely to be imitated by competitors over time. This reality underscores the importance of generating continuous improvements and novel solutions. Accordingly, the ability to apply creativity and innovation in addressing challenges—commonly referred to as innovation capability—becomes essential for sustaining long- term success. In Indonesia, the innovation ability of SMEs has become an increasingly important factor in driving national economic growth. SMEs play a strategic role in creating employment and increasing household income. Nevertheless, organizational innovation capability has not yet received sufficient attention in the SME sector (Donbesuur et al., 2020; Heenkenda et al., 2022; Olaleye et al., 2024). Previous studies emphasize that achieving sustainable organizational performance requires fostering innovation across all levels of the firm, thereby strengthening competitiveness in the global marketplace (Oduro, 2024; Wang & Zhang, 2025). Therefore, SMEs should prioritize strengthening their innovation capability by developing entrepreneurial knowledge, adopting new technologies, and enhancing competencies as strategic measures to sustain their market position. Empirical studies on innovation capability in both large organizations and SMEs generally demonstrate a positive and significant relationship between innovation capability and business performance (Aljuboori et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2022; Le et al., 2020; Migdadi, 2022; Purwati et al., 2020; Siahaan & Tan, 2020; Sulistyo & Ayuni, 2020). However, other studies have reported evidence of a negative association between the two constructs (Le et al., 2023; Zhang, 2022). These inconsistent findings underscore the need for further empirical investigation, particularly in the context of SMEs. Although prior studies have examined the relationship between innovation and SME performance, few have specifically focused on the differentiated effects of product, process, and market innovation capability within the manufacturing sector of developing economies such as Indonesia. In addition, inconsistent findings on the effectiveness of product innovation, combined with the scarcity of regional studies employing structural equation modelling (SEM), underscore a clear research gap. To address this gap, the present study investigates the role of innovation capability and its dimensions in influencing SME performance. On the basis of the introduction, the following hypotheses are proposed: H1: Product innovation capability has a positive and significant effect on SME performance. H2: Process innovation capability has a positive and significant effect on SME performance. H3: Market innovation capability has a positive and significant effect on SME performance. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Participants and procedure This study involved 160 owners or managers of manufacturing SMEs operating in Batu city, East Java, Indonesia. The participants were selected via purposive sampling to ensure that only individuals directly involved in innovation-related decision-making and business operations were included. The respondents represented various manufacturing subsectors, including the agro-industry, food processing, and creative industries. A sample size of 160 was considered sufficient for statistical analysis, which is consistent with the recommendations of Hair et al. (2018) for multivariate research. Prior to data collection, approval was obtained from the local SME association. The questionnaires were then distributed directly to the respondents. This method was chosen for its efficiency and ability to minimize interviewer bias. The participants completed the questionnaires independently, requiring approximately 15–20 minutes. All completed questionnaires were collected and checked for completeness before data entry and analysis. 2.2. Measurement of variables Primary data were collected via structured self-administered questionnaires, which allow for the efficient collection of large amounts of data within a short period. These instruments are widely used because they are cost effective in obtaining primary data from relatively large populations (Bell et al., 2022). Innovation capability was measured via 12 items adapted from Songkajorn et al. (2020). A 5-point Likert scale option was used to answer the statement items in the questionnaire. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”). The innovation capability dimensions and items are shown in Table 1. SME performance was assessed via five items adapted from Islami (2021) and Migdadi (2022), covering both financial performance (profit and sales volume) and nonfinancial performance (production costs, product quality, and customer service). These items were also measured on a five-point Likert scale. To analyse the data, structural equation modelling (SEM) with Smart-PLS 4.0 was employed to evaluate the effects of the independent variables on the dependent variable and to test the proposed hypotheses. Discussion This study examines the influence of three dimensions of innovation capability—product, process, and market innovation—on the performance of SMEs in the manufacturing sector in Batu city, East Java, Indonesia. The hypotheses were evaluated via PLS‒SEM, and the results revealed mixed support for the proposed relationships. 4.1. Product innovation capability and SME performance The results indicate that product innovation capability does not have a significant effect on SME performance. This suggests that, in the studied context, product innovation capability alone does not directly lead to improved performance outcomes due to several contextual limitations. Many SMEs in developing countries face constraints in terms of financial resources, technological infrastructure, and skilled human capital, which hinder their ability to effectively implement and scale new product ideas. Moreover, the benefits of product innovation often require time to materialize and may not be immediately reflected in short-term performance indicators. In some cases, new products may not align with consumer needs or market demand, reducing their commercial viability. These findings align with those of previous studies (Farida & Nuryakin, 2021; Yulianto & https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Setyawati et al. (2026) 6 Supriono, 2023), which argue that product innovation processes are costly, high risk, and difficult to sustain for SMEs that prioritize short-term survival over long-term innovation (Migdadi, 2022). In addition, the Indonesian market is largely price sensitive, meaning that consumers tend to prefer affordable and functional products over more innovative but higher-priced alternatives (Yulianto & Supriono, 2023). Weak protection of intellectual property rights further reduces the long-term advantage of product innovations, as new ideas can be easily imitated by competitors (Migdadi, 2022). Thus, while product innovation remains an essential component of business strategy, its direct effect on SME performance is limited if not complemented by strong marketing capabilities, efficient production processes, and a deeper understanding of consumer behavior. Interestingly, this result contrasts with findings from other contexts (Jorge & Coelho, 2020; Keelson et al., 2024), which reported significant positive effects of product innovation on firms. These differences underscore the importance of contextual factors—such as institutional support, market characteristics, and resource availability—in shaping the relationship between product innovation and SME performance. 4.2. Process innovation capability and its impact on SME performance Hypothesis 2 (H2) is supported. The results confirm that process innovation capability has a significant positive effect on SME performance. This finding indicates that improvements in business processes can enhance product quality, customer service, workflow efficiency, resource utilization, and market responsiveness, ultimately leading to better service delivery and increased competitiveness in dynamic environments. These results align with earlier studies (Gill & Hanafi, 2020; Rumanti et al., 2022; Yulianto & Supriono, 2023), which demonstrated that innovation capabilities—particularly process innovation—play a critical role in strengthening SME performance. Similarly, Heenkenda et al. (2022) emphasized that process innovation is especially valuable for SMEs in emerging economies, as it tends to be more cost-effective, less resource intensive, and able to generate immediate performance benefits than other types of innovation are. Nevertheless, these findings contrast with those of Kiguru (2022), who reported that process innovation did not significantly influence SME performance. Such differences highlight the role of contextual factors, including industry characteristics, technological adoption levels, and institutional support, in shaping the extent to which process innovation translates into measurable performance outcomes. In the Indonesian context, where SMEs often operate with limited resources, focusing on process innovation may provide a more practical and impactful pathway to enhance competitiveness than investing heavily in product innovation. 4.3. Market innovation capability and its impact on SME performance Hypothesis 3 (H3) is supported. The results demonstrate that market innovation capability has a significant positive effect on SME performance. This finding indicates that the ability of SMEs to refine, adapt, and target specific market segments strongly influences performance outcomes, particularly by enhancing product quality, customer service, and overall market responsiveness. By aligning marketing strategies with customer needs, SMEs are able to strengthen brand loyalty, improve satisfaction, and ensure that their offerings remain relevant in highly dynamic markets. These findings are consistent with previous research (Tali et al., 2021; Heenkenda et al., 2022), which emphasized the critical role of market innovation in enabling SMEs to remain competitive, maintain consistent product excellence, and adapt to evolving consumer expectations. They also align with dynamic capabilities theory, which underscores the importance of continuously reconfiguring organizational resources to respond effectively to environmental changes. In the context of Indonesian SMEs, where financial and technological resources are often limited, market innovation has emerged as a pragmatic and cost-effective strategy to achieve competitiveness without necessitating substantial investments in new product development. Thus, prioritizing market innovation is not only a strategic imperative but also a key determinant of long-term sustainability and growth for SMEs. 5. Conclusion This study investigated the influence of multidimensional innovation capabilities—comprising product, process, and market innovations—on the performance of manufacturing SMEs in Indonesia. The results reveal that while process and market innovation capabilities significantly enhance SME performance, product innovation capability does not have a statistically significant effect. These findings suggest that, within the Indonesian SME context, improving operational efficiency and strengthening market responsiveness are more critical drivers of performance than the introduction of new products. 6. Research Implications This research extends the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capabilities theory by demonstrating that not all dimensions of innovation capabilities contribute equally to firm outcomes, particularly in resource-constrained environments. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Setyawati et al. (2026) 7 The nonsignificant role of product innovation likely reflects contextual limitations, such as insufficient technological infrastructure, weak intellectual property protection, or limited market readiness. From a practical perspective, the study highlights that SME managers should prioritize investments in process improvements and market-oriented strategies, such as optimizing production workflows, enhancing customer responsiveness, and tailoring offerings to consumer needs, rather than allocating excessive resources to new product development, which often entails high costs and risks. Nevertheless, this study is subject to several limitations. Its cross-sectional design, focus on a single industrial sector, and concentration in one geographic area may restrict the generalizability of the findings. In addition, the reliance on self- reported performance data raises the possibility of response bias. Future research should adopt longitudinal approaches, investigate other industries and regions, and incorporate moderating factors such as digital transformation, leadership behavior, or organizational learning to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how innovation capabilities shape SME performance over time. JSON: Name: sme_innovation_plssem Title: PLS-SEM assessment of the effects of product, process, and market innovation capabilities on SME performance in the Indonesian manufacturing sector Short Hypothesis: Higher process and market innovation capabilities cause increased SME performance in manufacturing small and medium enterprises. Related Work: Prior research on innovation capability and SME performance predominantly uses cross-sectional survey designs analyzed with variance-based SEM (PLS-SEM) or covariance-based SEM. Existing studies show mixed findings: many report positive links between aggregated innovation capability and firm performance, while others find weak or null effects for product innovation. Current approaches frequently rely on small, regionally constrained samples, self-reported performance metrics, and reflective-only measurement models. Common limitations include limited causal identification from cross-sectional designs, susceptibility to common-method bias, inconsistent operationalization of innovation dimensions, limited use of objective financial data, sparse treatment of control variables and moderators (e.g., digital adoption, firm size), and inadequate sensitivity or robustness analyses (e.g., alternative estimators or ablation tests). Comparative evaluations between PLS-SEM and CB-SEM or regression approaches are rare, and few studies perform measurement invariance or multi-group analyses across subsectors. These gaps reduce generalizability and leave the differentiated roles of product, process, and market innovation insufficiently resolved. Abstract: This research addresses whether distinct innovation capability dimensions—product, process, and market—drive measurable performance improvements in manufacturing SMEs. We propose a quantitative assessment using structural equation modeling to estimate direct effects of each innovation capability dimension on firm performance while improving on prior work through larger sample size, inclusion of objective financial indicators, and robustness comparisons across estimators. The main contribution is a disaggregated, validated measurement model and an empirical evaluation that distinguishes the relative explanatory power and effect sizes of process, market, and product innovation capabilities. Expected outcomes include precise estimates of path coefficients, R2 improvements attributable to each capability, and identification of which dimensions yield substantive performance gains in resource-constrained SME settings. The results aim to inform managerial prioritization and policy targeting by clarifying which innovation investments are empirically associated with near-term performance improvements in emerging-market manufacturing SMEs. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Primary survey dataset of manufacturing SMEs in East Java, Indonesia; target N = 300–500 owners/managers covering agro-industry, food processing, and creative subsectors; instruments: 12 innovation-capability items (product/process/market) and 5 performance items; 5-point Likert responses. 2) Secondary administrative dataset: firm-level objective financials where available (annual sales, profit, production cost) for a subsample (minimum N = 150) matched to survey respondents. Baselines: A) Original PLS-SEM model with three exogenous constructs (product, process, market) predicting SME performance. B) CB-SEM specification of equivalent latent-variable model. C) OLS regression with aggregated indices. D) Nested models removing one predictor at a time (ablation: remove product, remove process, remove market). E) Extended models adding controls (firm size, firm age, subsector) and moderators (digital adoption score). Evaluation metrics: measurement-level: indicator loadings, AVE, composite reliability (CR), HTMT; structural-level: path coefficients, bootstrap t-statistics (5,000 resamples), p-values, R2, f2 effect sizes, Q2 predictive relevance, SRMR, model comparison via AIC/BIC for CB-SEM and PLSpredict for out-of-sample predictive checks. Experimental setup: perform item-level CFA and reliability tests, test common-method bias via Harman's single-factor and marker-variable methods, test collinearity (VIF), run PLS-SEM in SmartPLS and R (plssem or semPLS), run CB-SEM in lavaan; conduct multi-group analysis by subsector and measurement invariance test; ablation study: record ΔR2 and change in key path coefficients when each innovation dimension is removed; sensitivity analysis: vary sample by bootstrapped subsamples, compare results using subjective vs objective performance measures, and report statistical power and minimum detectable effects. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: measurement model mis-specification leading to biased path estimates; multicollinearity among innovation dimensions inflating standard errors; inadequate model identification for CB-SEM if indicators or sample size are insufficient. Data and evaluation biases: reliance on self-reported performance introduces common-method and social-desirability bias; nonresponse and purposive sampling generate selection bias limiting representativeness; matching survey to administrative financials may reduce effective sample and introduce survivorship bias. Scalability and compute: bootstrap-based inference and multi-group tests with large numbers of items may be computationally intensive but feasible on standard research workstations; CB-SEM fit and estimation may fail if distributional assumptions are violated. Limits to generalization: results may not transfer beyond Indonesian manufacturing SMEs or to service sectors; cross-sectional design constrains causal inference and temporal ordering; heterogeneity across subsectors and informal firms may limit external validity. Ethical and data availability constraints: financial records may be incomplete or withheld for confidentiality, reducing objective-measure coverage.
